text: Good morning everyone. Today I want to talk about the future of renewable energy and why it matters to each and every one of us. This is a topic that will shape our world for generations to come. Let me start by giving you some background on where we stand today. According to the International Energy Agency, renewable energy accounted for nearly thirty percent of global electricity generation in 2023. Solar and wind power have seen dramatic cost reductions over the past decade, with solar panel costs dropping by nearly ninety percent since 2010. These are not just numbers on a page. They represent a fundamental shift in how we power our civilization. Now let me share a personal story. Three years ago I visited a small village in rural India that had just received its first solar microgrid. Before that, children studied by candlelight. Businesses could not operate after dark. The transformation was remarkable. Within months, a small clinic opened with reliable power for refrigeration. Students improved their test scores. New businesses emerged. One solar installation changed the economic trajectory of an entire community. But we need to look at the data more carefully. The intermittency problem remains real. Wind does not always blow. The sun does not always shine. Current battery technology can store energy for hours, but seasonal storage remains expensive. A study by MIT found that achieving one hundred percent renewable energy would require massive overinvestment in generation capacity or breakthrough storage technology. The cost estimates range from two to five times current electricity prices without storage innovation. Some critics argue that nuclear energy is a better path forward. They point to its reliability and small land footprint. This is a fair point that deserves consideration. However, the construction timelines for nuclear plants have averaged ten to fifteen years in Western countries, and costs have consistently exceeded initial estimates. The Hinkley Point C project in the UK is a case study in nuclear cost overruns. I want to leave you with this thought. The question is not whether we will transition to clean energy. The question is how fast and how smartly we do it. Every year of delay means more carbon in the atmosphere, more extreme weather events, and higher eventual costs. I urge each of you to consider what role you can play. Whether it is installing solar panels on your roof, supporting clean energy policies, or simply educating others about the options available. Together, we can accelerate this transition and build a more sustainable future for our children and grandchildren. Thank you.
